title: The Clipboard Spy
content:
When you copy something — a password, an account number, a message — it sits in your phone's clipboard. For years, many apps could quietly read it.

In 2020, when iPhones started showing a small "pasted from" alert, people noticed dozens of popular apps, including TikTok and LinkedIn, reading the clipboard. Both said they would stop.

Phones are safer now: iPhones show an alert or ask your permission, and Android (version 12 and newer) shows a message when an app reads your clipboard. Older phones that no longer get updates have less protection.

How to protect yourself:

→ Don't copy your PIN, passwords or one-time codes if you can avoid it

→ Use your phone's password manager to fill in passwords instead of copy and paste

→ On iPhone: Settings → choose an app → Paste from Other Apps → Ask

→ If you see a "pasted from" alert you didn't expect, ask why that app needs it

Report scams to the Cyber Security Authority: call or text 292, or WhatsApp 0501603111.

title: When Your Phone Wakes Up by Mistake
content:
Voice assistants like "Hey Google" and "Hey Siri" listen for their wake words. Sometimes they get it wrong — a word on TV or in a conversation sounds close enough, and they start recording.

Researchers and the companies themselves have confirmed these accidental wake-ups happen. Separately, any app you've given microphone permission can use the mic while it's allowed to.

Good news: newer phones show a small coloured dot or icon at the top of the screen when the microphone or camera is in use.

How to protect yourself:

→ Watch for the microphone dot — if it appears and you're not using the mic, find out which app it is

→ On iPhone: Settings → Privacy & Security → Microphone

→ On Android: Settings → search "Permission manager" → Microphone

→ Take mic access away from apps that don't need it

→ Switch off the voice assistant's wake word if you never use it

Report scams to the Cyber Security Authority: call or text 292, or WhatsApp 0501603111.

title: The "Significant Locations" Map
content:
Your phone can keep a list of places you visit often — home, work, church, the clinic.

On iPhone it's called "Significant Locations". Apple says it is encrypted and kept on your device, and it is used for things like travel-time suggestions. On Android, Google Maps "Timeline" saves your visits if you switched it on — and Google now keeps new Timeline data on your phone rather than online.

It's not a secret, but most people have never looked. Anyone who can unlock your phone could see it.

How to check:

→ iPhone: Settings → Privacy & Security → Location Services → System Services → Significant Locations

→ Android: open Google Maps → tap your picture → Your Timeline

→ Clear the history or switch it off if you don't use it

→ Keep a strong screen lock, so nobody else can browse this

Report scams to the Cyber Security Authority: call or text 292, or WhatsApp 0501603111.

title: Apps That Know Where You Are All Day
content:
When an app asks for your location, you can usually choose "only while using the app" or "all the time". Choose "all the time" and the app can check where you are even when you're not using it.

Many apps don't need this. Some collect location to show you adverts, and some pass it on to other companies.

Both iPhone and Android now remind you when an app has been using your location in the background — but only if you read those reminders.

How to protect yourself:

→ Set location to "While using the app" or "Never" for most apps

→ iPhone: Settings → Privacy & Security → Location Services

→ Android: Settings → Location → App location permissions

→ Check the privacy report: "App Privacy Report" on iPhone, "Privacy dashboard" on Android

→ Delete apps you no longer use

Report scams to the Cyber Security Authority: call or text 292, or WhatsApp 0501603111.

title: The Bluetooth Beacon in the Shop
content:
Some shops and malls, mostly abroad, place small Bluetooth "beacons" on their shelves. They send out a signal. An app on your phone — usually the shop's own app — can notice the signal and tell the shop you are near a certain section.

Your phone doesn't do this by itself. It needs Bluetooth switched on and an app that you've allowed to look for nearby devices.

How to protect yourself:

→ Switch Bluetooth off when you're not using it

→ Don't give shopping apps "Nearby devices" or "Bluetooth" permission unless you need it

→ Check which apps can see nearby devices: Settings → Privacy (iPhone) or Permission manager (Android)

→ Delete shop apps you no longer use

Report scams to the Cyber Security Authority: call or text 292, or WhatsApp 0501603111.

title: The App Quietly Eating Your Battery
content:
Your phone used to last all day. Now it's hot and empty by afternoon, even when you hardly use it.

Batteries do get weaker with age. But a sudden change can also mean an app is working hard in the background — and sometimes that app is harmful, sending your data or showing hidden adverts.

How to check:

→ Open Settings → Battery to see which apps use the most power

→ An app you rarely open near the top of that list is a warning sign

→ Also check mobile data use (Settings → Network or Mobile data) for apps using a lot of data

→ Delete apps you don't recognise or don't need

→ Install apps only from the Play Store or App Store, and keep your phone updated

If your phone stays hot, slow and drained after removing apps, ask a trusted repair shop to check the battery.

Report scams to the Cyber Security Authority: call or text 292, or WhatsApp 0501603111.

title: The Little Green Dot
content:
See a small green or orange dot at the top of your phone screen? That's your phone telling you the camera or microphone is in use right now.

iPhones (since iOS 14) and Android phones (since Android 12) show these dots. If one appears when you're not taking a photo or a call, an app is using your camera or mic.

Laptop cameras usually have a small light. In 2013, researchers showed that some older laptop webcams could be switched on without the light — a reason many people cover their laptop camera.

How to protect yourself:

→ When you see the dot, swipe down from the top to see which app is using it

→ Take camera and microphone access away from apps that don't need it

→ Install apps only from official app stores

→ A simple sticker or slide cover on a laptop camera costs almost nothing

title: Spy Apps That Read What You Type
content:
There are apps made to secretly watch a phone — they can record what you type, read your chats and track your location. They're sometimes called "stalkerware".

Most of the time, these apps are installed by someone who has had your unlocked phone in their hands, like a jealous partner. Some harmful apps also abuse Android's "Accessibility" feature to read your screen.

Warning signs: your phone runs hot or slow, battery or data drains fast, or someone knows things they shouldn't.

How to protect yourself:

→ Use a screen lock (PIN or fingerprint) and don't share it

→ Don't leave your phone unlocked with others

→ On Android: Settings → Accessibility — check for apps you don't recognise there

→ Install apps only from official app stores

→ If you think someone is spying on you, get help from someone you trust before removing it — the person may notice

Report scams to the Cyber Security Authority: call or text 292, or WhatsApp 0501603111.

title: Wi-Fi Scanning in the Background
content:
Even when you switch Wi-Fi off, many Android phones still scan for nearby Wi-Fi networks. It's a setting called "Wi-Fi scanning", and it helps the phone work out your location more accurately.

Phones also look for networks you've joined before. Older phones used to send out a fixed ID while doing this, which could be used to track them. Newer phones use a random ID, which makes this much harder.

How to protect yourself:

→ On Android: Settings → Location → Location services → switch off Wi-Fi scanning and Bluetooth scanning

→ Remove ("forget") old Wi-Fi networks you no longer use

→ Keep your phone updated, so it gets the newer privacy protections

Report scams to the Cyber Security Authority: call or text 292, or WhatsApp 0501603111.

title: The "Off" State Myth
content:
"Powered off" isn't always as off as you'd assume.

On modern phones, a few low-level components can stay partly awake even when the screen is dark — that's how features like "Find My" or Bluetooth tracker tags can still be located while the phone appears off. This isn't a secret spy mode; it's a documented design choice, and on most phones you can see and control much of it in settings.

What's actually worth knowing:

→ "Sleep" and "low-power" states keep some radios and timers running so alarms, find-my-device, and quick wake-up still work

→ A genuinely powered-down phone does far less — but truly powering off (not just locking) is still the simplest way to go quiet

→ The realistic risk for most people isn't secret government tracking; it's everyday apps you've granted location and background permissions to

What you can actually do:

→ Power the phone fully off when you want it silent, rather than relying on airplane mode alone

→ Review which apps have "always" location and background access, and cut the ones that don't need it

→ Keep your software updated — that's where real security fixes land

You don't need a Faraday bag to have privacy. You need to know what your apps are allowed to do — and to switch the phone off when you mean off.
